workload.description: Managed API gateway in front of a function tier; 80% reads, 20% writes

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: t4g.medium — AWS EC2 us-east-1 / On-Demand / Linux / shared tenancy / 730 h per month; instance-hour only (excludes EBS, data transfer); arm64 (Graviton2), BURSTABLE. Band: zero-width: within the pinned scope the hourly list rate is a single exact published number with no variance. Month length (672-744 h), burstable credit surcharges, Savings Plans and Spot are OUT-OF-BAND modifiers, named per row, not band edges.

citations.note: $0.0336/h x 730 = 2453c/month. Cross-checked to the cent against the AWS Price List Bulk API (version 20260904231117). BURSTABLE: launches in Unlimited mode by default; sustained above-baseline CPU adds $0.04/vCPU-hour (Price List SKU VQE3NKNEDMWWG8DZ). At sustained 100% CPU the real bill can reach ~2.9x this figure. Disclosed, deliberately NOT folded into the band.

monthly_cost_per_instance.measured_context: cache.t4g.medium — AWS ElastiCache us-east-1 / On-Demand / Redis engine / standard support / 730 h per month; node-hour only. Band: zero-width at the Redis/Memcached standard-support rate. The Valkey engine is CHEAPER and Extended Support is DEARER; both are different products/support states, not a price range for this row, so they are named here rather than used as band edges.

db.t4g.medium — AWS RDS PostgreSQL us-east-1 / On-Demand / Single-AZ (band high = Multi-AZ) / 730 h per month; INSTANCE-HOURS ONLY (excludes storage, provisioned IOPS and backup above the free allocation). Band: deployment spread: low = Single-AZ, high = Multi-AZ. Both are on-demand, standard-tier, us-east-1 PostgreSQL, so the band is fully in scope. Multi-AZ is ~2x Single-AZ.

citations.note: $0.065/h Single-AZ x 730 = 4745c/month. MySQL/MariaDB run ~3.9% cheaper than PostgreSQL for the same class.

assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 1,500 req/s peak, 80:20 read:write. Monthly request volume assumes an average of 300 req/s (20% of peak) = 777.6M gateway requests/month

assumptions.subject: fn
assumptions.statement: THE ENGINE HAS NO SERVERLESS COMPONENT KIND. The function tier is modelled as an app_server whose capacity is its CONCURRENCY CEILING (4 units x ~500 req/s), which is the shape that actually constrains a Lambda-style API. Cold starts, per-invocation billing and burst-concurrency limits are NOT modelled

assumptions.subject: fn
assumptions.statement: Compute is priced from the provisioned-instance catalogue (t4g.medium x4), i.e. the cost of holding that concurrency warm. Pure per-invocation pricing would be cheaper at low duty cycle and dearer at high; treat the compute line as an upper bound

assumptions.subject: db
assumptions.statement: The engine has no key-value/document kind, so the item store is modelled as `sql_db` — the persistent record store on the path. 5,000 req/s stands for provisioned read/write capacity, not a Postgres primary

assumptions.subject: cache
assumptions.statement: 80% hit-rate on single-item reads, 50% on list queries (list results go stale faster)

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: The API gateway is the dominant line: at $3.00 per million requests, 777.6M requests/month is roughly $2,330 — several times the compute bill. That is the real trade-off of the serverless shape, not a modelling artefact

assumptions.subject: cost
assumptions.statement: The $3.00-per-million request rate is applied to the API GATEWAY only, which is the kind it was measured for. Object-store request charges are left out: S3's per-request price is an order of magnitude lower and the engine carries only one request rate

_library.summary: Managed API gateway fronting a function tier, a hot-item cache and a key-value store.
